Video 1 / 4 · Sound 주아쌤 · Soritune English · Short 0:59 · in Korean

English sits further back in the voice

영어는 발성 위치가 다르다: 입 앞이 아니라 더 뒤에서 울린다

  1. Front vs. back. Korean comes mostly from the front of the mouth. English resonates further back; the coach describes it as sound that forms in the chest. 한국어: 입 앞에서 · 영어: 뒤쪽, 가슴에서 맺히는 느낌
  2. Same letters, different sound. A native speaker's "파도" comes out deeper and more open, with a puff of air on the p [pʰ]. Even "아" is not quite the Korean 아.
  3. Why it helps listening. If your ear expects bright, front-of-mouth Korean sounds, English vowels can sound muffled or swallowed. Knowing where the sound lives tells your ear what to expect, and sounds you can make yourself are easier to hear.

Try it · 30 seconds

Say 파도 the Korean way. Now drop your jaw, relax your throat and let air out on the p: "PHA-do". Hold a tissue in front of your mouth: it should move on PHA. A hand on your chest should feel more buzz.

Coach's note

"Chest voice" is a teaching image, not a phonetics term. What really changes is a more open jaw, stronger puffs of air, relaxed vowels and lots of schwa /ə/. Linguists call a language's default mouth posture its articulatory setting (조음 기저).

Video 2 / 4 · Sound Tiffany (Girls' Generation) · 소녀시대연구소 · Short 1:00 · Korean + song

One singer, two voice settings

같은 사람, 같은 노래인데 발성이 다르다

  1. Her rule. In Korean the sound comes very far forward; in English it "sits back." "한국어로 할 때는 소리가 굉장히 앞으로 나와 있고, 영어로 할 때는 뒤로 앉는다"
  2. Bilinguals switch the whole setting. Tiffany grew up in the US. She doesn't only swap words: resonance, airflow and rhythm all change with the language.
  3. A perfect listening test. She sings a song from the musical Chicago in Korean and in English. Same singer, same melody, so every difference you hear comes from the language itself.

Try it · watch three times

1 Just listen. 2 Write down three differences in the English version (darker vowels? more air? words joined together?). 3 Hum along, then shadow (섀도잉) a few words right after her.

Coach's note

Songs are great ear training: melody slows the words down and repeats them. But singing stretches vowels and moves stress to fit the beat, so always check the same words in normal speech too.

Video 3 / 4 · Rhythm Keith O'Hare · English Speaking Success · 11:26 · in English

Catch the stressed words, not every word

모든 단어를 들으려 하지 말고, 강세 받는 단어를 잡아라

  1. The #1 mistake: trying to catch every word. You fall behind and give up. Go for the gist first. (요지 = 전체 뜻)
  2. Sentence stress (문장 강세): nouns, main verbs, adjectives and adverbs are loud and long; small words like in, a, to go short and quiet.
  3. A steady beat (강세 박자): stresses come at regular intervals and extra syllables get squeezed in. Natives listen this way too: key words + context + a guess.

Same beat, more syllables

●●●● ILIVEin aTOWNnearLONdon· I've beenLIVingin thisTOWNjust nearLONdonforYEARS
  • Stress changes meaning: a town NEAR London = not far · "NO, I live in a town near London" = you're wrong

His 5 practice tips

  • 1Micro-dictation: 2–3 sentences, 3 passes, then check
  • 2Long listening: no dictionary, no notes
  • 3Expect gaps: nobody hears everything
  • 4One hour a day, in pieces
  • 5Subtitles off sometimes

Coach's note

The strongest of the four. One addition: squeezed words don't vanish, they become weak forms (to → /tə/, and → /ən/, can → /kən/). Learning them fills the gaps (next slide, then slide 7).

Deep dive · Pronunciation Rachel's English · Friends scene · 31:52 · in English

One real scene, taken apart sound by sound

〈프렌즈〉 40초 장면을 한 줄씩: 강세를 찾고, 작은 단어가 어떻게 변하는지 듣기

  1. One peak per thought. "So I don't think I should DO it anymore." Words lead up to the peak and fall away after it, flatter and quicker: slide 4's beat in real speech.
  2. Small words bend. Unstressed words link, shrink and lose sounds. In American English, T alone makes four sounds: true (terrible), flap (pot is), stop (don't care: like a 받침, no 트) and dropped (jus' don't).

Video 4 / 4 · Habit EngFluent · 5:39 · in English

Make it convenient, or you'll quit

편해야 오래 하고, 오래 해야 는다

  1. Why most people fail. Listening improves over months, but people choose tiring methods (rewatching movies, writing everything down) and quit before results show.
  2. Step 1: load up. Put lots of natural, unscripted conversation on your phone: real people really talking.
  3. Step 2: use dead time (자투리 시간). Listen while commuting, waiting in line or exercising, so it costs no extra time.

Coach's note

Volume matters, but only for audio you can follow. Background audio you don't understand is just noise, so pick material where you know about 95% of the words. Save dead time for tasks that leave your attention free (walking, yes; writing email, no). And keep 10 focused minutes for dictation (video 3), even though this video calls it too much work.

Beyond the videos suggested additions

What the videos miss: 6 methods to add

영상에서 다루지 않은 6가지 보완 방법

1Connected speech 연음·축약

At speed, words blend: linking, weak forms, gonna, flap t. This is usually why you "know the words but can't hear them." See the table →

2Shadowing 섀도잉

Repeat 1–2 sentences a split second behind the speaker, copying rhythm and melody. Use the transcript first, then go without. It trains sound and rhythm together.

3Right difficulty 적정 난이도

Choose audio where you already know about 95% of the words. Harder is just noise; easier gives no growth.

4Minimal pairs, many voices 최소대립쌍

Quiz yourself on pairs Korean ears tend to merge (f/p, v/b, l/r, ship/sheep) spoken by many different speakers. Well researched as HVPT.

5Narrow listening 좁게 많이 듣기

5–10 short clips on one topic or from one speaker. Words and accent repeat, so understanding climbs fast.

6Subtitle ladder 자막 사다리

Subtitles off by default. When stuck, rewind and peek at English subtitles (never Korean), then replay without. Slow to 0.75× only for focused work.

can vs. can't: in American English, can is weak and quick (/kən/) while can't is stressed (/kænt/). Listen for the stress, not the t.

Putting it together all the videos + slide 7

A two-track daily routine

하루 루틴: 집중 듣기 15분 + 많이 듣기 45분

Track A · Focused 집중 듣기 · 10–15 min at a desk

One clip of 30–60 seconds:

  1. Gist: listen once and say the main idea. video 3
  2. Dictate ×3: stressed words → more → everything. video 3
  3. Check the transcript. For each miss: new word, or connected speech? slides 5 · 7
  4. Shadow it 3–5 times, voice set further back. videos 1–2
  5. Listen again. It will sound slower than the first time.

Track B · Volume 많이 듣기 · 30–45 min in dead time

Easy, natural audio (about 95% known words). No pausing, no dictionary. Stay with one show or topic for a week (narrow listening). video 4 · slide 7

Weekly check 주간 점검

Every Sunday, replay Monday's Track A clip with no transcript and count the words you catch. That number going up is your progress.

A sample day

07:40Commutepodcast episode, same show all weekB · 20 min
12:30Walk after lunchreplay yesterday's episodeB · 10 min
19:30At a deskone clip, the full 5-step loopA · 15 min
22:30Before bedeasy audio, screen offB · 15 min
60 min a day: Keith's target ~15 min of free time: EngFluent's rule

Appendix A · Culture Tyler Rasch · One Big World Show · Short 1:20 · in Korean

Korean marks nuance with particles; English uses stress

한국어는 조사로, 영어는 억양과 표현으로 뉘앙스를 바꾼다

  1. Two systems. Korean shifts nuance with small particles like 은/는. English is an analytic language: to add nuance you change your intonation or your words. (영어는 분석어)
  2. His example. After a tough team project, you tell an outsider: "저는 진짜 노력을 많이 한 거 같아요." The 는 can quietly leave your teammates out: I worked hard, maybe they didn't.
  3. In English: "It was a really hard project, but, you know, I think I made a lot of effort to get it done." No 는, so no comparison, and nobody feels left out.

Try it · one sentence, three meanings

Say "I made a lot of effort" three times, stressing a different word: I (unlike the others, like 저는) · LOT (how much) · EFfort (neutral). Then listen for which one a speaker uses.

Why it's in a listening deck

Korean listeners often hunt for hidden meaning in plain English sentences. In English, contrast is mostly heard, not written: it lives in the stressed word, exactly what slide 4 trains. A stressed pronoun ("I did it") is the closest English match to contrastive 는.

Appendix B · Mindset Tyler Rasch · One Big World Show · 14:00 · in Korean

A new language is a new way of seeing

외국어는 소통 수단이 아니라, 세상을 보는 또 하나의 방식(인지 환경)이다

  1. More than a tool. "AI translates, so why learn?" treats language as a tool. Tyler's answer: a new language expands your cognitive environment (인지 환경), how you perceive the world and yourself.
  2. Learning is like swimming. Beginner: splashing in the shallows. Intermediate: snorkeling, where grammar gets hard but you can travel and chat. Advanced: scuba, with a long plateau and then discoveries nobody on the beach can imagine.
  3. Languages steer attention. His examples: Westerners call a photo "a plane", East Asians "an airport". One Aboriginal Australian community lays out time east to west, whichever way they face. Matsés speakers must mark how they know a fact, so a bare "I have five apples" sounds like a lie.
  4. Korean ↔ English. Humble hedging that works in Korean ("Well, I guess it's kind of like…") can sound unprepared in an English seminar.

For your listening

The intermediate plateau is normal. Past it is "deep water": unscripted talk, jokes, hedging and indirectness. Advanced listening means hearing what someone means, not only what they say.

Coach's note

The examples come from real research (Nisbett's The Geography of Thought, Lera Boroditsky on time, studies of Matsés). But language nudges attention rather than locking thought, and the claim that learning languages boosts creativity is still debated.

Appendix C · Habit Tyler Rasch · One Big World Show · 15:14 · in Korean

Subtitles give away the answer, so your ears stop working

영어 자막을 켜면 정답이 보이니, 뇌가 들을 필요가 없어진다

  1. Study vs. learn (공부 vs 배움). Memorized lines are study: "How are you?" → "I'm fine, thank you, and you?" To learn (배우다, from 배다, to soak in) is to use the language until it's part of you. Age isn't the barrier; your environment is.
  2. Three conditions for acquiring any language: exposure (노출), motivation (동기), you want it, and necessity (필요성), you can't get by without it.
  3. Why subtitles break it. A hard word comes, your eyes drop, and the answer is written there. Exposure and motivation stay, but necessity is gone: "like learning to walk on crutches."
  4. The fix. Subtitles off. When you're really stuck, rewind, peek once, get the "aha", and switch them off again.

His other tips

  • 1i+1: content one step above your level (Krashen)
  • 2Play right away: 5 letters already make bad, bed, dead
  • 3Design your environment: set your phone to English

Coach's note

This matches Keith's tip 5 (slide 4), and slide 7's subtitle tip now agrees with it. One correction: he calls the critical period hypothesis "fake". Age effects are real, especially for accent, but adults can still reach a high level, and environment matters more for most learners.
